answer.sourceLine: From the “Apology for Raymond Sebond,” the longest essay in Montaigne’s Essais (Book II, Ch. 12), first published 1580. The French reads “Il ne sçauroit forger un ciron, et forge des Dieux à douzaines”; this familiar English wording is Charles Cotton’s translation.

source.excerpt: Man is certainly stark mad; he cannot make a worm, and yet he will be making gods by dozens.
trail: Listed in Wikiquote’s Sourced section, cited to Book II, Ch. 12 (“Apology for Raimond Sebond”) via Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919).
The French original — “L’homme est bien insensé. Il ne sçauroit forger un ciron, et forge des Dieux à douzaines” — is confirmed in the ATHENA text from Essais II.12.
The familiar English wording is Charles Cotton’s 17th-century translation, the version reproduced across quotation catalogues such as LibQuotes.
source.excerptNote: Montaigne’s French “ciron” is a mite — the tiniest creature then visible to the eye. Cotton loosely rendered it “worm”; later translators (e.g. Donald Frame) keep “mite”: “he could not make a mite, and he makes gods by the dozen.” The thought — man cannot fashion the smallest living thing yet manufactures deities wholesale — is Montaigne’s in every version.

source.rightsNote: Both the French original (1580) and Charles Cotton’s English translation (1685–86, revised by W. C. Hazlitt in 1877) were published well before 1931 and are in the public domain in the United States.

author.heading: Who was Montaigne?
author.metaLine: 1533–1592 · French Renaissance philosopher & inventor of the essay
author.bio: Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592) was a French nobleman, magistrate, and writer who all but invented the personal essay with his Essais (1580–1595). Skeptical, digressive, and relentlessly self-examining, he made his own doubt the instrument of inquiry — the “Apology for Raymond Sebond” is his longest and most corrosive attack on human presumption, of which this line is a signature barb.

misattribution.heading: The wording, honestly
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is right — this really is Montaigne. The only thing worth flagging is that the memorable English is a translator’s work, not Montaigne’s own words.

items.why: The crisp English — “stark mad… make a worm… gods by dozens” — is Charles Cotton’s 17th-century rendering. Montaigne wrote “Il ne sçauroit forger un ciron, et forge des Dieux à douzaines.”
Montaigne’s “ciron” is a mite — the smallest visible creature — not a worm; modern translations such as Donald Frame’s keep “mite.”

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Montaigne, from Essais II.12; the exact English you see is Charles Cotton’s translation.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In the “Apology for Raymond Sebond,” Montaigne mounts a sweeping case against human arrogance — the conviction that our reason grasps the cosmos. The jab about worms and gods is his method in miniature: set man’s vast metaphysical ambition beside his inability to fashion the humblest living thing, and the presumption collapses into comedy.
The thought echoed forward: Pascal, who read Montaigne closely, folds this very contrast between human littleness and human pretension into the Pensées.
